Run the commands yourself

Microbiome workshop: step-by-step analysis

A complete run of the workflow from raw 16S reads to diversity statistics: each command, what it printed, every plot, and how to read them.

The data set: 30 samplescondition C1 condition C2
Study G1

99% identity

99% identity

99% identity
Study G5
S15S16S24S01S20S30
97% identity

Five study groups, each with three samples per condition. Sample names are neutral codes. One group was filtered at a different identity threshold, so compare groups with care.

How to use this page

  1. This is the worked answer: every command of the workflow with the output and plots from a complete test run.
  2. Each numbered step shows the R code first and what it printed underneath. Long outputs are folded; select Show to open them.
  3. Coloured boxes explain the idea behind a section; captions under the plots explain how to read them.
  4. Your own numbers should match these if you used the same data and seed. Small differences in file paths and timings are normal.

Read this before interpreting anything

The reads were selected because they match a bacterial reference panel, each comparison has three samples per condition, and one study group used a different identity threshold. Treat every result as exploratory: good for learning the method, not for biological conclusions.

Set up the workshop

The idea. Before any analysis, R needs its packages, the right copy of mothur for your computer, and the data unpacked into a fresh folder. Nothing biological happens yet; this section makes sure everyone in the room starts from exactly the same files.

  • Packages. phyloseq stores microbiome data, vegan calculates diversity and distances, ggplot2 and patchwork draw and combine plots.
  • Checksums. Lines with digest(..., algo = "sha256") compute a fingerprint of a file and compare it with the expected one. If a download was cut short or a file was edited, the fingerprints differ and stopifnot() halts the run instead of letting you analyse damaged data.
  • Run folder. Each run gets its own time-stamped folder under runs/, so you can repeat the workshop without overwriting earlier work.
  • reads.files. A three-column table (sample, forward file, reverse file) that tells mothur which two FASTQ files belong to each sample.

Run the commands in order in RStudio. Press Copy and paste the complete command. Package preparation is a prerequisite.

1

Set the working directory to the workshop folder. The path is found automatically, so nothing needs to be typed.

Every later command uses paths such as scripts/, metadata/ and vendor/ that are relative to the workshop folder. If R is already there (as it is when you knit, or when the folder is open as an RStudio project), nothing changes. Otherwise the folder is taken from workflow.Rmd open in RStudio; if that is not possible, a file window opens and you select workflow.Rmd in the workshop folder. The stopifnot() line stops with an error if the folder is not the right one, and getwd() prints the folder in use.

R code
if (!file.exists("workflow.Rmd")) {
  open_file <- if (requireNamespace("rstudioapi", quietly = TRUE) && rstudioapi::isAvailable())
    rstudioapi::getSourceEditorContext()$path else ""
  if (!nzchar(open_file) || basename(open_file) != "workflow.Rmd") open_file <- file.choose()
  setwd(dirname(normalizePath(open_file)))
}
stopifnot(file.exists("workflow.Rmd"), dir.exists("scripts"), dir.exists("vendor"))
getwd()
2

Install and check the required packages.

R code
source("scripts/prepare_packages.R")
Output
Checking R packages in a separate process. Please keep RStudio open.
Output
Package setup finished. Open workflow.Rmd and run its chunks from the top.
3

Check that every package the workflow needs is installed, then load them all. This is the only cell that loads packages; no later step calls library().

The preparation command, source("scripts/prepare_packages.R"), already installs anything that is missing. This cell confirms it worked: if a package is absent it stops with the package name instead of failing later with a confusing error. phyloseq stores the data, vegan calculates diversity and PERMANOVA, ggplot2 and patchwork draw the figures, MetaQC checks whether the studies can be combined, ANCOMBC tests differential abundance and metafor runs the meta-analyses.

R code
packages <- c("phyloseq", "vegan", "ggplot2", "patchwork", "ANCOMBC", "metafor", "MetaQC", "jsonlite", "digest", "processx")
missing_packages <- packages[!vapply(packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) stop("Not installed: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "), ". Run source(\"scripts/prepare_packages.R\") again.")
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ANCOMBC)
library(metafor)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(MetaQC))
4

Check the supplied files.

R code
manifest <- jsonlite::read_json("resources.json", simplifyVector = TRUE)
5

Read the operating system.

R code
system_name <- Sys.info()[["sysname"]]
6

Read the R processor architecture.

R code
architecture <- ifelse(tolower(R.version$arch) %in% c("aarch64", "arm64"), "arm64", "x86_64")
7

Choose the mothur archive for this system.

R code
asset <- switch(system_name, Darwin = paste0("Mothur.OSX_", architecture, ".zip"), Linux = paste0("Mothur.linux_", architecture, ".noReadline.zip"), Windows = if (architecture == "x86_64") "Mothur.win.zip" else stop("Windows ARM is not supported"), stop("Unsupported operating system"))
8

Confirm the mothur archive is unchanged.

R code
stopifnot(digest::digest(file = file.path("vendor", asset), algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE) == manifest$resources$sha256[match(asset, manifest$resources$name)])
9

Create a folder for mothur.

R code
runtime_dir <- file.path(".tools", sub("\\.zip$", "", asset))
10

Create the program folder.

R code
dir.create(runtime_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
11

Extract mothur.

R code
utils::unzip(file.path("vendor", asset), exdir = runtime_dir)
12

Locate the program.

R code
mothur <- normalizePath(list.files(runtime_dir, pattern = if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") "^mothur\\.exe$" else "^mothur$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)[1], mustWork = TRUE)
13

Allow the program to run on macOS and Linux.

R code
if (.Platform$OS.type != "windows") Sys.chmod(mothur, "0755")
14

Allow mothur’s helper programs to run.

R code
if (.Platform$OS.type != "windows") Sys.chmod(list.files(dirname(mothur), pattern = "^(vsearch|uchime)$", full.names = TRUE), "0755")
15

Make the helper programs available.

R code
Sys.setenv(PATH = paste(dirname(mothur), Sys.getenv("PATH"), sep = .Platform$path.sep))
16

Choose a fresh analysis folder.

R code
run_dir <- file.path("runs", paste0("teaching-", format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")))
17

Create the analysis folder.

R code
dir.create(run_dir, recursive = TRUE)
18

Use its full path.

R code
run_dir <- normalizePath(run_dir, mustWork = TRUE)
19

Verify the read archive.

R code
stopifnot(digest::digest(file = "vendor/workshop_reads.zip", algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE) == manifest$workshop_reads_sha256)
20

Extract the anonymized reads.

R code
utils::unzip("vendor/workshop_reads.zip", exdir = run_dir)
21

Read the sample list.

R code
sample_summary <- read.delim(file.path(run_dir, "filtered_fastq", "summary.tsv"))
22

Create the paired-read manifest.

R code
read_manifest <- data.frame(sample = sample_summary$sample_id, forward = paste0("filtered_fastq/", sample_summary$sample_id, "_R1.fastq.gz"), reverse = paste0("filtered_fastq/", sample_summary$sample_id, "_R2.fastq.gz"))
23

Save the paired-read manifest for mothur.

R code
write.table(read_manifest, file.path(run_dir, "reads.files"), sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)
24

Verify the SILVA archive.

R code
stopifnot(digest::digest(file = "vendor/silva.bacteria.zip", algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE) == manifest$resources$sha256[match("silva.bacteria.zip", manifest$resources$name)])
25

Extract the SILVA reference.

R code
utils::unzip("vendor/silva.bacteria.zip", exdir = run_dir)
26

Place the alignment where mothur can find it.

R code
stopifnot(file.copy(file.path(run_dir, "silva.bacteria", "silva.bacteria.fasta"), file.path(run_dir, "silva.bacteria.fasta")))
27

Verify the taxonomy training archive.

R code
stopifnot(digest::digest(file = "vendor/trainset9_032012.pds.zip", algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE) == manifest$resources$sha256[match("trainset9_032012.pds.zip", manifest$resources$name)])
28

Extract the taxonomy training files.

R code
utils::unzip("vendor/trainset9_032012.pds.zip", exdir = run_dir)

Run mothur commands one by one

The idea. mothur is a separate program for processing 16S rRNA gene sequences. Here R starts one mothur session and sends it one command at a time, so you can read what each command prints before moving on.

mothur remembers the most recent file of each type. That is why many commands say fasta=current and count=current: "use whatever the last step produced". After every command, get.current() lists those remembered files; reading that list is the quickest way to check that a step did what you expected.

File names grow as you go. reads.trim.contigs.good.unique.fasta reads from left to right as a history: contigs were made, bad ones removed (good), duplicates collapsed (unique).

In this recorded run the log was sometimes read a moment before mothur had finished writing. An output block can therefore show the messages of the command just before it.

Each command runs in the active mothur session. The following small R steps wait for it and print the output in the Console before you start the next command. A diagnostic get.current command shows the files available to mothur.

29

Choose where to save the mothur output.

R code
mothur_log <- file.path(run_dir, "mothur-console.log")
30

Start one persistent mothur session from R.

R code
mothur_process <- processx::process$new(mothur, stdin = "|", stdout = mothur_log, stderr = "2>&1", wd = run_dir, cleanup = TRUE)
31

Start tracking output already shown in the Console.

R code
mothur_cursor <- 0L

Assemble and screen reads

Goal of this stage. Turn each pair of raw reads into one clean sequence. The forward and reverse reads overlap in the middle of the amplicon; joining them gives a longer, more accurate sequence called a contig. Then sequences that are obviously faulty are discarded and identical sequences are collapsed so later steps run faster.

32

Set the number of processors set.current

mothur > set.current(processors=4)

Tells mothur how many processor cores it may use. More cores make the slow steps (alignment, distances) faster. Nothing is analysed yet.

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("set.current(processors=4)\nget.current()\n")
Helper R steps: wait, print, check for errors, remember position

Wait until this mothur command has completed.

R code
repeat { Sys.sleep(0.2); mothur_output <- readLines(mothur_log, warn = FALSE); if (sum(grepl("Current files saved by mothur:", mothur_output, fixed = TRUE)) >= 1) break; if (!mothur_process$is_alive()) stop("Mothur stopped before completing the command") }

Print this mothur command’s output in the Console.

R code
cat(paste(mothur_output[seq.int(mothur_cursor + 1L, length(mothur_output))], collapse = "\n"))

Stop if this command reported an error.

R code
stopifnot(!any(grepl("[ERROR]", mothur_output[seq.int(mothur_cursor + 1L, length(mothur_output))], fixed = TRUE)))

Remember the output already displayed.

R code
mothur_cursor <- length(mothur_output)

34

Join forward and reverse reads make.contigs

mothur > make.contigs(file=reads.files)

Reads the sample list in reads.files and merges each read pair into one contig. Where the two reads overlap and disagree, the base with the better quality score wins. Output: one FASTA file with all contigs and a count table recording which sample each came from.

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("make.contigs(file=reads.files)\nget.current()\n")
Helper R steps: wait, print, check for errors, remember position

Wait until this mothur command has completed.

R code
repeat { Sys.sleep(0.2); mothur_output <- readLines(mothur_log, warn = FALSE); if (sum(grepl("Current files saved by mothur:", mothur_output, fixed = TRUE)) >= 3) break; if (!mothur_process$is_alive()) stop("Mothur stopped before completing the command") }

Print this mothur command’s output in the Console.

R code
cat(paste(mothur_output[seq.int(mothur_cursor + 1L, length(mothur_output))], collapse = "\n"))

Stop if this command reported an error.

R code
stopifnot(!any(grepl("[ERROR]", mothur_output[seq.int(mothur_cursor + 1L, length(mothur_output))], fixed = TRUE)))

Remember the output already displayed.

R code
mothur_cursor <- length(mothur_output)

Nothing new had reached the log when this step printed. The messages from this command appear in the next output block.

35

Summarise the contigs summary.seqs

mothur > summary.seqs(fasta=current,count=current)

Prints a table describing the sequences: where they start and end, their length (NBases), ambiguous bases (Ambigs) and the longest run of one repeated base (Polymer). Check: most lengths should be close together. Very long contigs usually mean the two reads did not overlap properly.

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("summary.seqs(fasta=current,count=current)\nget.current()\n")
Helper R steps: wait, print, check for errors, remember position

Wait until this mothur command has completed.

Print this mothur command’s output in the Console.

Remove poor contigs screen.seqs

mothur > screen.seqs(fasta=current,count=current,maxambig=0,minlength=400,maxlength=550,maxhomop=8)

Discards contigs with any ambiguous base (maxambig=0), contigs shorter than 400 or longer than 550 bases, and contigs with a run of more than 8 identical bases (maxhomop=8). These are almost always sequencing or assembly errors. Run this block once: it stops with a message if the screened file already exists.

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("screen.seqs(fasta=current,count=current,maxambig=0,minlength=400,maxlength=550,maxhomop=8)\nget.current()\n")

Collapse identical sequences unique.seqs

mothur > unique.seqs(fasta=current,count=current)

Trim the reference and align

Goal of this stage. Line every sequence up against a reference alignment (SILVA) so that position 100 in one sequence corresponds to position 100 in every other. Only aligned sequences can be compared fairly. The reference is first trimmed to the region these reads cover, which makes alignment much faster.

optimize=start-end, criteria=95 finds the start and end positions that 95% of sequences share and removes sequences that start later or end earlier. What remains overlaps the same part of the gene. Run this block once: it stops with a message if the screened file already exists.

Filter and classify

Goal of this stage. Remove the remaining noise and give each sequence a name. Sequences that differ by only a few bases from a much more abundant one are treated as sequencing errors and merged; chimeras (artificial sequences made of two parents during PCR) are removed; each surviving sequence is classified against a taxonomy training set; and anything that is not a bacterium is dropped.

47

Remove empty alignment columns filter.seqs

mothur > filter.seqs(fasta=current,vertical=T,trump=.)

vertical=T deletes columns that contain only gaps. trump=. deletes any column where at least one sequence has no data. The alignment becomes much shorter without losing information, and every sequence now spans exactly the same columns.

49

Merge likely sequencing errors pre.cluster

mothur > pre.cluster(fasta=current,count=current,diffs=4)

Within each sample, a rare sequence that differs by up to 4 bases (diffs=4, about 1 per 100 bases) from a more abundant one is assumed to be an error and merged into it. This removes much of the noise that would otherwise inflate diversity.

50

Find and remove chimeras chimera.vsearch

mothur > chimera.vsearch(fasta=current,count=current,dereplicate=t)

A chimera is an artificial sequence created during PCR when a half-copied fragment finishes on a different template. VSEARCH looks for sequences that are explained by joining two more abundant ones. dereplicate=t removes a flagged sequence only from the samples where it was flagged.

R code that sends the command

Assign taxonomy to each sequence classify.seqs

mothur > classify.seqs(fasta=current,count=current,reference=trainset9_032012.pds.fasta,taxonomy=trainset9_032012.pds.tax)

Compares each sequence with the RDP training set using a naive Bayesian classifier and reports the best lineage from kingdom to genus. The number in brackets after each rank is the bootstrap confidence (0–100).

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("classify.seqs(fasta=current,count=current,reference=trainset9_032012.pds.fasta,taxonomy=trainset9_032012.pds.tax)\nget.current()\n")
Helper R steps: wait, print, check for errors, remember position

Wait until this mothur command has completed.

R code
repeat { Sys.sleep(0.2); mothur_output <- readLines(mothur_log, warn = FALSE); if (sum(grepl("Current files saved by mothur:", mothur_output, fixed = TRUE)) >= 21) break; if (!mothur_process$is_alive()) stop("Mothur stopped before completing the command") }

Print this mothur command’s output in the Console.

R code

Stop if this command reported an error.

R code
stopifnot(!any(grepl("[ERROR]", mothur_output[seq.int(mothur_cursor + 1L, length(mothur_output))], fixed = TRUE)))

Create feature and diversity tables

Goal of this stage. Count features per sample. The same cleaned sequences are grouped in three ways so you can compare them: OTUs (sequences at least 97% similar), ASVs (every unique sequence is its own feature) and phylotypes (grouped by taxonomic name). The result of each is a shared file: a table with one row per sample and one column per feature. mothur then calculates sample depth, rarefaction curves, alpha diversity and between-sample distances.

56

Calculate distances between sequences dist.seqs

mothur > dist.seqs(fasta=final.fasta,cutoff=0.03)

Computes the fraction of positions that differ for every pair of sequences. cutoff=0.03 stores only pairs that differ by 3% or less, since larger distances are not needed for 97% OTUs.

R code that sends the command
mothur_process$write_input("dist.seqs(fasta=final.fasta,cutoff=0.03)\nget.current()\n")

Cluster sequences into OTUs cluster

mothur > cluster(column=final.dist,count=final.count_table)

Groups sequences into operational taxonomic units with the OptiClust algorithm so that sequences within an OTU are at most 3% different. An OTU is a practical stand-in for a species-level group.

Check your understanding

Answer in your head first, then open to compare.

Why are the forward and reverse reads joined into one contig before anything else?

Each read covers only part of the amplicon and read quality drops towards its end. The two reads overlap, so joining them gives the full region and lets the better-quality base win wherever they disagree.

What is a chimera, and why does it matter if chimeras stay in the data?

A chimera is an artificial sequence made from two different templates during PCR. It looks like a new organism that does not exist, so leaving chimeras in inflates the number of OTUs and the diversity.

The OTU table and the ASV table are built from the same sequences. Why do they have different numbers of columns?

An OTU groups all sequences within 3% of each other, while every unique sequence is its own ASV. Several ASVs therefore usually fall into one OTU, so the ASV table has more columns.

Import the results

The idea. mothur is finished; from here everything happens in R. The OTU count table, the taxonomy and the sample metadata are read in, checked against each other, and combined into one phyloseq object so that counts, sample information and taxonomy always stay in step.

Build a phyloseq object from the completed mothur tables and anonymous metadata.

All five studies side by side

The idea. The five studies are analysed together in this chapter, in four steps:

  1. Quality control: reads per sample, then MetaQC, which scores how homogeneous (IQC) and consistent (CQC) the studies are and decides which can be combined.
  2. Alpha and beta diversity of the included studies, shown side by side.
  3. ANCOM-BC per study: the effect size (log fold change) and standard error of every OTU, estimated separately in each study.
  4. Random-effects meta-analysis with metafor::rma(method = "REML"), which pools the per-study effect sizes into one result per OTU, followed by a cladogram and the pooled effect on alpha diversity.

Keep in mind. Each study has three samples per condition. These analyses teach the method; they cannot prove a difference.

What the side-by-side analysis showed

MetaQC: studies included
4 of 5 G4 excluded: fails IQC (1.56 < 2.0) and CQCg
Alpha diversity (four indices, four studies)
0 of 16 comparisons below p = 0.05; smallest p = 0.1
PERMANOVA (four distances, four studies)
0 of 16 below p = 0.05; R² from 0.04 to 0.31
ANCOM-BC estimates (per study)
41 usable of 51; 1 with p < 0.05, 0 with q < 0.05
OTUs pooled with the random-effects model
7 of 19 tested
Otu16 Streptococcus: pooled log fold change
+1.21 95% CI 0.34 to 2.09, adjusted p = 0.046

MetaQC excluded one of the five studies. In the four that remain, no single study shows a significant difference in any analysis. Pooling them with a random-effects model finds one OTU, Otu16 Streptococcus, higher in C2: it points the same way in all three studies where it could be tested. Otu05 is close (p = 0.058) but depends on whether G5 is included. With three samples per group the standard errors are themselves uncertain, so these are leads to follow up, not confirmed results.

Settings, colours and one table per study

The idea. The five studies are first checked with MetaQC; every later figure shows the studies that pass next to each other, with the two conditions inside each study. The colours and the plain black-framed panels follow the figures of the reference paper (Marzouk et al., npj Parkinson's Disease 2025): salmon for the first condition, teal for the second, and olive for taxa that are not significant.

All packages were loaded once, in a single cell earlier on this page, so no library() call is needed here.

Split the counts and metadata into one piece per study, with the three C1 samples first and the three C2 samples last.

Each piece holds the metadata (m), the counts (mat) and the relative abundances (relative) of one study. Every later step loops over these pieces, so one command analyses all studies. After MetaQC the list keeps only the included studies.

R code
study_data <- lapply(setNames(studies, studies), function(s) {
  m <- metadata[metadata$study == s, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- m[order(m$condition), , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(nrow(m) == 6, all(table(m$condition) == 3))
  mat <- count_matrix[rownames(m), , drop = FALSE]
  list(m = m, mat = mat, relative = mat / rowSums(mat))
})

Set the random seed so that every run gives the same numbers.

R code
set.seed(20261114)

Quality control: reads per sample

Why quality control comes first. Before comparing conditions, check that every sample has enough reads to be trusted. A sample with very few reads shows fewer OTUs simply because less was sequenced, not because the community is poorer. Look for two things: samples far below the others within a study, and studies that differ strongly from each other in depth. Both affect richness (Observed, Chao1) and presence/absence distances (Jclass) most, and they are one reason why the studies are later pooled with a random-effects model, which allows studies to differ.

101

Count the reads of every sample.

R code
qc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(studies, function(s) {
  d <- study_data[[s]]
  data.frame(study = s, sample_name = rownames(d$m), condition = d$m$condition, reads = rowSums(d$mat))
}))
write.csv(qc, file.path(out_dir, "qc_by_study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

  geom_col(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~study, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colours) +
  labs(title = "Reads per sample after mothur", x = "Sample", y = "Reads", fill = "Condition") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

print(qc_plot)

MetaQC: can the studies be combined?

Why MetaQC. A meta-analysis only makes sense if the studies measure comparable things. MetaQC (Kang et al., Nucleic Acids Research 2012; R package by Don Kang and George Tseng) gives every study a score on six quality measures and so turns the decision to include or exclude a study into an objective rule. It was written for gene-expression studies; here the “genes” are OTUs and the “pathways” are taxonomic groups (phylum, class, order, family, genus).

  • IQC (internal quality control): is the co-abundance structure of the study (which OTUs rise and fall together) similar to that of the other studies? This is the homogeneity check.
  • EQC (external quality control): do OTUs of the same taxonomic group co-vary more than random OTUs?
  • CQCg / CQCp (consistency quality control): does the study rank OTUs (g) and taxonomic groups (p) by their C1-versus-C2 difference in the same order as the other studies combined?
  • AQCg / AQCp (accuracy quality control): does the study find the same significant OTUs or groups as the other studies combined?

How to read a score. Each score is −log10(p-value): higher is better. With K studies a score passes when it is above −log10(0.05/K), which is 2.0 for five studies. MetaQC marks scores below that line with an asterisk (*). The Rank column is the mean rank of a study over the six measures; lower is better.

The decision rule used here. IQC (homogeneity) and CQC (consistency) are the two measures that decide. A study is excluded when it fails both IQC and CQCg; all other studies go on to the diversity analyses, ANCOM-BC and the meta-analysis.

Keep in mind. MetaQC was designed for thousands of genes and larger groups. With 10 to 17 OTUs and three samples per condition, the consistency and accuracy measures (CQC, AQC) cannot reach significance in any study, so the decision rests mainly on IQC.

103

Prepare the MetaQC input. For every study, log-ratio transform the counts (CLR) and keep the OTUs seen in at least two of its six samples.

MetaQC expects continuous values, like expression levels. The centred log-ratio (CLR) turns counts into such values and removes the effect of sequencing depth. MetaQC takes a list with one element per study: x holds the OTUs in rows and the samples in columns, y the condition of each sample.

R code
metaqc_input <- lapply(study_data, function(d) {
  present <- d$mat[, colSums(d$mat > 0) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  clr <- log(present + 1)
  clr <- clr - rowMeans(clr)
  keep <- colSums(present > 0) >= 2 & apply(clr, 2, var) > 0
  list(x = t(clr[, keep, drop = FALSE]), y = as.character(d$m$condition))
})
sapply(metaqc_input, function(d) nrow(d$x))
Output
G1 G2 G3 G4 G5 
13 12 10 17 16

Write the taxonomic groups in the GMT format that MetaQC reads for its pathway-based measures (EQC, CQCp, AQCp).

Each line of a GMT file is one group: its name, a description, then its members. Every phylum, class, order, family and genus with at least two OTUs becomes one group.

R code
metaqc_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "metaqc")
dir.create(metaqc_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
taxon_sets <- unlist(lapply(c("Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus"), function(rank)
  split(rownames(tax_matrix), paste(rank, tax_matrix[, rank], sep = "_"))), recursive = FALSE)
taxon_sets <- taxon_sets[lengths(taxon_sets) >= 2 & !duplicated(taxon_sets)]
writeLines(vapply(names(taxon_sets), function(n) paste(c(n, "taxonomy", taxon_sets[[n]]), collapse = "\t"), character(1)),
           file.path(metaqc_dir, "taxon_sets.gmt"))
lengths(taxon_sets)

105

Adapt the IQC calculation to small tables.

MetaQC computes IQC by comparing the OTU-by-OTU correlations of every pair of studies. To save memory with thousands of genes it repeats this 100 times on a random 10% of the shared genes. With about ten shared OTUs, 10% is a single OTU and no correlation can be computed, so this function does the same comparison once on all shared OTUs. Everything else in MetaQC is used unchanged.

R code
iqc_all_shared <- function(.) {
  pairs <- combn(length(.$.DListF), 2)
  distance <- apply(pairs, 2, function(ii) {
    shared <- intersect(rownames(.$.DListF[[ii[1]]]$x), rownames(.$.DListF[[ii[2]]]$x))
    correlations <- sapply(1:2, function(j) as.vector(as.dist(cor(t(.$.DListF[[ii[j]]]$x[shared, , drop = FALSE])))))
    correlations <- na.omit(correlations)
    (1 - cor(correlations[, 1], correlations[, 2], method = "spearman")) / 2
  })
  m <- matrix(0, length(.$.DListF), length(.$.DListF), dimnames = list(names(.$.DListF), names(.$.DListF)))
  m[t(pairs)] <- distance
  m[t(pairs[2:1, ])] <- distance
  .$.DistOfStudies <- as.dist(m)
}
106

Run MetaQC: create the MetaQC object, plug in the IQC function and compute all six measures with 10,000 permutations.

MetaQC writes helper files in the working directory, so the run happens inside the metaqc output folder and R returns to the workshop folder afterwards. registerDoSEQ() tells MetaQC to run on one core.

R code
foreach::registerDoSEQ()
run_metaqc <- function() {
  old_dir <- setwd(metaqc_dir)
  on.exit(setwd(old_dir))
  set.seed(20261114)
  object <- MetaQC(metaqc_input, "taxon_sets.gmt", filterGenes = FALSE, minNumGenes = 2, verbose = FALSE)
  object$.CalcDistOfStudies <- iqc_all_shared
  suppressWarnings(runQC(object, B = 1e4, fileForCQCp = "taxon_sets.gmt"))
  object
}
metaqc <- run_metaqc()
metaqc$Print()

Apply the decision rule: exclude a study that fails both IQC and CQCg, and keep the others for every later step.

From here on, studies and study_data hold only the included studies, so the alpha and beta diversity, ANCOM-BC and the meta-analysis all use the quality-controlled set.

metaqc_decision <- data.frame(study = rownames(metaqc_scores), IQC = round(metaqc_scores$IQC, 2), CQCg = round(metaqc_scores$CQCg, 2),
                              passes_IQC = metaqc_scores$IQC >= metaqc_threshold, passes_CQCg = metaqc_scores$CQCg >= metaqc_threshold)
metaqc_decision$included <- metaqc_decision$passes_IQC | metaqc_decision$passes_CQCg
metaqc_decision <- metaqc_decision[order(metaqc_decision$study), ]
write.csv(metaqc_decision, file.path(out_dir, "metaqc_decision.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(metaqc_decision, row.names = FALSE)
excluded_studies <- metaqc_decision$study[!metaqc_decision$included]
studies <- setdiff(studies, excluded_studies)
study_data <- study_data[studies]
studies

Alpha diversity: Observed, Chao1, Shannon and Inverse Simpson

What it measures. Diversity within one sample.

  • Observed: how many different OTUs are present (richness).
  • Chao1: an estimate of the true richness. It adds to the observed count an estimate of the OTUs that were missed, based on how many OTUs were seen only once or twice. If no OTU is seen only once, Chao1 equals Observed.
  • Shannon: richness and evenness together.
  • Inverse Simpson: the effective number of dominant OTUs; it gives more weight to the abundant ones.

Keep in mind. With three samples per condition, an exact two-sided test cannot give a p-value below 0.1.

110

Calculate the four alpha-diversity indices for every sample.

estimateR() from vegan returns Chao1 in its row S.chao1; diversity() returns Shannon and Inverse Simpson.

R code
alpha <- do.call(rbind, lapply(studies, function(s) {
  d <- study_data[[s]]
  data.frame(study = s, sample_name = rownames(d$mat), condition = d$m$condition,
             observed = rowSums(d$mat > 0),
             chao1 = estimateR(d$mat)["S.chao1", ],
             shannon = diversity(d$mat, "shannon"),
             inverse_simpson = diversity(d$mat, "invsimpson"))
}))
write.csv(alpha, file.path(out_dir, "alpha_by_study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(alpha, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

111

Write the exact permutation test: compare the observed C2-minus-C1 difference with all 20 ways of splitting six samples into two groups of three.

R code
allocations <- combn(6, 3)
exact_test <- function(x) {
  observed <- mean(x[4:6]) - mean(x[1:3])
  permuted <- apply(allocations, 2, function(i) mean(x[-i]) - mean(x[i]))
  c(difference = observed, p = mean(abs(permuted) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12))
}

  r <- exact_test(alpha[alpha$study == s, metric])
  data.frame(study = s, metric = metric, difference_C2_minus_C1 = r[["difference"]], p_value = r[["p"]])
}))))

Beta diversity: Bray–Curtis, Canberra, Jclass and ThetaYC

What it measures. How different two samples are from each other. Four distances are used, the same calculators that mothur offers in dist.shared:

  • Bray–Curtis: based on abundances; dominated by the common OTUs.
  • Canberra: based on abundances, but every OTU counts equally, so rare OTUs matter as much as common ones.
  • Jclass (Jaccard): uses only presence or absence. It answers “do the two samples contain the same OTUs?”
  • ThetaYC (Yue & Clayton): compares the community structure, that is the proportions of shared and unshared OTUs.

PCoA. Each distance matrix is turned into a map in which similar samples sit close together. The percentage on each axis is the share of the total variation that the axis shows.

PERMANOVA asks whether the condition explains part of the distances (R²). PERMDISP asks whether one condition is simply more spread out than the other, which can make PERMANOVA misleading. Both tests are exact here: with six samples vegan can try every possible reordering of the samples instead of a random selection. There are only 20 ways to split six samples into two groups of three, so the smallest possible PERMANOVA p-value is 1/20 = 0.05.

114

Write the ThetaYC distance, which vegan does not include.

For two samples with relative abundances a and b: 1 − Σab / (Σa² + Σb² − Σab).

R code
thetayc <- function(relative) {
  cross <- relative %*% t(relative)
  squares <- diag(cross)
  as.dist(1 - cross / (outer(squares, squares, "+") - cross))
}
115

List the four distances. Each entry is a small function that takes one study and returns its distance matrix.

R code
distance_functions <- list(
  "Bray-Curtis" = function(d) vegdist(d$relative, method = "bray"),
  "Canberra"    = function(d) vegdist(d$relative, method = "canberra"),
  "Jclass"      = function(d) vegdist(d$mat, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
  "ThetaYC"     = function(d) thetayc(d$relative))
116

For every distance and every study: run the PCoA, the PERMANOVA and the PERMDISP test.

cmdscale() is the PCoA; its eigenvalues give the percentage of variation on each axis. adonis2() is PERMANOVA, and betadisper() with permutest() is PERMDISP. Both ask for 999 permutations, but with six samples there are only 720 possible orderings, so vegan tries every one of them and the tests are exact; suppressMessages() hides the note that says so. It is written vegan::permutest() because the metafor package has a function with the same name. suppressWarnings() hides a harmless note that vegan prints for distances that cannot be drawn exactly on flat axes.

R code
beta <- lapply(names(distance_functions), function(distance_name) lapply(studies, function(s) {
  d <- study_data[[s]]
  distance <- distance_functions[[distance_name]](d)
  pcoa <- cmdscale(distance, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
  explained <- 100 * pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
  permanova <- suppressMessages(adonis2(distance ~ condition, data = d$m, permutations = 999))
  permdisp <- suppressMessages(vegan::permutest(suppressWarnings(betadisper(distance, d$m$condition)), permutations = 999))
  list(points = data.frame(distance = distance_name, study = s, sample_name = rownames(d$m), condition = d$m$condition,
                           PCoA1 = pcoa$points[, 1], PCoA2 = pcoa$points[, 2]),
       tests = data.frame(distance = distance_name, study = s, axis1_percent = explained[1], axis2_percent = explained[2],
                          R2 = permanova$R2[1], F = permanova$F[1], permanova_p = permanova$`Pr(>F)`[1],
                          permdisp_p = permdisp$tab$`Pr(>F)`[1]))
}))
pcoa_points <- do.call(rbind, lapply(beta, function(x) do.call(rbind, lapply(x, `[[`, "points"))))
beta_tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(beta, function(x) do.call(rbind, lapply(x, `[[`, "tests"))))
write.csv(pcoa_points, file.path(out_dir, "pcoa_by_study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(beta_tests, file.path(out_dir, "permanova_by_study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

118

Write a function that returns the outline of an ellipse around the samples of one condition.

The ellipse is centred on the mean of the samples and follows their spread (their covariance); it covers about 68% of a normal distribution fitted to them. stat_ellipse() from ggplot2 needs at least four samples per group, so with three the ellipse is calculated here.

R code
ellipse_points <- function(points, level = 0.68) {
  xy <- as.matrix(points[, c("PCoA1", "PCoA2")])
  spread <- eigen(cov(xy), symmetric = TRUE)
  circle <- rbind(cos(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)), sin(seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)))
  outline <- t(colMeans(xy) + spread$vectors %*% (sqrt(pmax(spread$values, 0) * qchisq(level, 2)) * circle))
  data.frame(condition = points$condition[1], PCoA1 = outline[, 1], PCoA2 = outline[, 2])
}
119

Write a function that draws the PCoA of one distance, one panel per study, with the percentage of variation written on the x- and y-axis.

An ellipse is drawn around the samples of each condition. Every panel is its own ordination, so each has its own axis labels.

R code
pcoa_figure <- function(distance_name) {
  panels <- lapply(studies, function(s) {
    points <- pcoa_points[pcoa_points$distance == distance_name & pcoa_points$study == s, ]
    tests <- beta_tests[beta_tests$distance == distance_name & beta_tests$study == s, ]
    ellipses <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(points, points$condition), ellipse_points))
    ggplot(points, aes(PCoA1, PCoA2, colour = condition, fill = condition)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
      geom_polygon(data = ellipses, alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.5) +
      geom_point(size = 3) +
      geom_text(aes(label = sample_name), vjust = -1, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colours) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = condition_colours) +
      scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.2)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.2)) +
      labs(title = s,
           subtitle = sprintf("PERMANOVA R2 = %.2f, p = %.2f\nPERMDISP p = %.2f", tests$R2, tests$permanova_p, tests$permdisp_p),
           x = sprintf("PCoA1 (%.1f%%)", tests$axis1_percent), y = sprintf("PCoA2 (%.1f%%)", tests$axis2_percent),
           colour = "Condition", fill = "Condition") +
      theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8.5), panel.grid = element_blank())
  })
  wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 1, guides = "collect") +
    plot_annotation(title = paste(distance_name, "PCoA")) & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}

ANCOM-BC per study: effect size and standard error for every OTU

One study at a time. ANCOM-BC is run separately in each included study, never on a merged table, so that differences between studies (sequencing depth, filtering) cannot create false differences between conditions. From every study we keep, for each OTU, the effect size (log fold change) and its standard error (SE): exactly the two numbers the meta-analysis needs.

Why ANCOM-BC instead of LEfSe. LEfSe first needs a Kruskal–Wallis p-value below 0.05. With three samples per condition the smallest value that test can give is 0.0495, and after adjustment for multiple testing nothing passes, so LEfSe reported no OTU in any study whatever the LDA cut-off. LEfSe also gives a score without a standard error, which a meta-analysis cannot use.

What ANCOM-BC does. Sequencing gives relative abundances: if one OTU goes up, the others must appear to go down even if they did not change. ANCOM-BC estimates and removes this bias, then reports for each OTU its effect size, the log fold change between conditions, together with a standard error, a p-value and an adjusted p-value (q). The function used is ancombc2(), the current version in the ANCOMBC package; the reference paper also used ANCOM-BC.

How to read a value. A log fold change of 0 means no difference; +0.69 means about twice as abundant in C2; −0.69 means about half.

125

Run ANCOM-BC in every study and collect, for every OTU, the effect size (log fold change, C2 versus C1), its standard error, the p-value and the adjusted p-value.

OTUs seen in fewer than two samples of a study are left out before the model is fitted. ANCOM-BC returns no estimate (NA) for an OTU found in only one condition, and a p-value of exactly 1 for an OTU found in a single sample of each condition, because it cannot be tested. The column usable marks the estimates that can be trusted and carried forward.

R code
ancom <- do.call(rbind, lapply(studies, function(s) {
  d <- study_data[[s]]
  keep <- colSums(d$mat > 0) >= 2
  set.seed(20261114)
  fit <- suppressWarnings(suppressMessages(ancombc2(data = t(d$mat[, keep, drop = FALSE]), taxa_are_rows = TRUE,
           meta_data = d$m, fix_formula = "condition", group = "condition", p_adj_method = "BH",
           prv_cut = 0, lib_cut = 0, struc_zero = FALSE, pseudo_sens = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)))
  r <- fit$res
  data.frame(study = s, feature = r$taxon, lfc_C2_vs_C1 = r$lfc_conditionC2, se = r$se_conditionC2,
             W = r$W_conditionC2, p_value = r$p_conditionC2, q_value = r$q_conditionC2)
}))
ancom$taxon <- unname(taxon_label[ancom$feature])
ancom$usable <- is.finite(ancom$lfc_C2_vs_C1) & is.finite(ancom$se) & ancom$se > 0 & ancom$p_value < 1
126

Label each estimate: higher in C1, higher in C2, or not significant.

The label uses the unadjusted p-value, because with three samples per condition almost nothing can pass the adjusted threshold. The adjusted value (q) is kept in the table and shown in the figures.

R code
significance_level <- 0.05
ancom$direction <- ifelse(!ancom$usable | ancom$p_value >= significance_level, "Not significant",
                          ifelse(ancom$lfc_C2_vs_C1 > 0, "Higher in C2", "Higher in C1"))
ancom$direction <- factor(ancom$direction, levels = c("Higher in C1", "Higher in C2", "Not significant"))
direction_colours <- c("Higher in C1" = condition_colours[["C1"]], "Higher in C2" = condition_colours[["C2"]], "Not significant" = not_significant_colour)
write.csv(ancom, file.path(out_dir, "ancombc_by_study.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

Random-effects meta-analysis (metafor, REML) for every OTU

The idea. Each study is small, but there are several of them. ANCOM-BC gave, for each OTU in each study, an effect size (log fold change) and its standard error. A meta-analysis combines the study estimates of one OTU into one pooled effect size. It has two parts: a check of which estimates can be pooled, and the random-effects model (REM), fitted with metafor::rma(method = "REML"), which does the pooling.

This is a different check from MetaQC at the start of the chapter: MetaQC decided which studies are combined; this step decides which estimates of those studies can be used.

Part 1: which estimates can be pooled. A pooled result is only as good as what goes into it, so three checks come first.

  • Is each estimate usable? An estimate is kept only if ANCOM-BC could really test the OTU in that study: it has a log fold change, a standard error and a p-value. OTUs found in only one condition, or in a single sample of each condition, are left out.
  • Are there enough studies? An OTU is pooled only if at least three studies have a usable estimate. With one or two studies there is nothing to compare.
  • Are the studies comparable? MetaQC has already removed the study that was not homogeneous with the others. The remaining studies were processed with the same mothur pipeline and the same reference, so their OTUs mean the same thing. They still differ in read depth (see the first figure of this chapter) and in one filtering threshold (G5 used 97% identity). These differences are a reason to prefer a random-effects model and to check each result with one study left out.

Part 2: the random-effects model (REM). A fixed-effect model assumes that all studies measure exactly the same true effect and differ only by chance. A random-effects model is more realistic here: it assumes that each study has its own true effect, and that these true effects scatter around an average. That average is the pooled effect size.

  • Each study estimate = average effect + how far this study’s true effect is from the average + sampling error.
  • tau² is the variance of the true effects between studies. If tau² is 0 the random-effects model gives the same answer as the fixed-effect model.
  • REML. tau² is estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (method = "REML"), the default in metafor. With few studies, plain maximum likelihood underestimates tau²; REML corrects for that.
  • Each study gets the weight 1 / (standard error² + tau²). Precise studies count more, but a large tau² makes the weights more equal, so no single study dominates.
  • estimate is the weighted average of the study effect sizes, with a 95% confidence interval. An interval that includes 0 is compatible with no difference.
  • I² is the percentage of the total variation that comes from real differences between studies and not from chance; the Q test asks whether there is more variation than chance alone would give. These two are the quality control of the pooled result itself.

Two OTUs are first worked through by hand so that you can see every step. Then one function repeats exactly the same steps for all OTUs.

130

Before pooling: for every OTU, list which studies give a usable estimate and whether the OTU can be pooled.

“usable” means ANCOM-BC could test the OTU in that study; “not testable” means the OTU was present but in too few samples; “not detected” means it was seen in fewer than two samples of that study. An OTU needs at least three usable studies.

R code
qc_meta <- expand.grid(feature = unique(ancom$feature), study = studies, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
found <- match(paste(qc_meta$feature, qc_meta$study), paste(ancom$feature, ancom$study))
qc_meta$status <- ifelse(is.na(found), "Not detected", ifelse(ancom$usable[found], "Usable", "Not testable"))
qc_meta$taxon <- unname(taxon_label[qc_meta$feature])
qc_summary <- as.data.frame.matrix(table(qc_meta$taxon, factor(qc_meta$status, levels = c("Usable", "Not testable", "Not detected"))))
qc_summary$pooled <- ifelse(qc_summary$Usable >= 3, "yes", "no")
write.csv(qc_meta, file.path(out_dir, "meta_qc.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(qc_summary)

All OTUs: write one function that does for any OTU what the two examples did by hand.

The quality-control rule is built in: an OTU is pooled only if at least three studies have a usable estimate; otherwise it is recorded as not estimable (NA). The function also returns tau², I² and the p-value of the Q test, so the heterogeneity of every pooled result can be checked.

R code
pool_otu <- function(feature) {
  d <- ancom[ancom$feature == feature & ancom$usable, ]
  not_estimable <- data.frame(feature = feature, studies = nrow(d), estimate = NA, se = NA, ci_lower = NA, ci_upper = NA,
                              p_value = NA, tau_squared = NA, I_squared = NA, Q_p_value = NA)
  if (nrow(d) < 3) return(not_estimable)
  model <- tryCatch(rma(yi = lfc_C2_vs_C1, sei = se, data = d, method = "REML"), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(model)) return(not_estimable)
  data.frame(feature = feature, studies = model$k, estimate = as.numeric(coef(model)), se = model$se, ci_lower = model$ci.lb,
             ci_upper = model$ci.ub, p_value = model$pval, tau_squared = model$tau2, I_squared = model$I2, Q_p_value = model$QEp)
}
140

All OTUs: apply the function to every OTU, adjust the p-values for multiple testing and save the table.

R code
meta_otu <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(ancom$feature), pool_otu))
meta_otu$adjusted_p <- p.adjust(meta_otu$p_value, "BH")
meta_otu$taxon <- unname(taxon_label[meta_otu$feature])
meta_otu$direction <- ifelse(is.na(meta_otu$p_value) | meta_otu$p_value >= significance_level, "Not significant",
                             ifelse(meta_otu$estimate > 0, "Higher in C2", "Higher in C1"))
meta_otu$direction <- factor(meta_otu$direction, levels = names(direction_colours))
meta_otu <- meta_otu[order(meta_otu$p_value), ]
write.csv(meta_otu, file.path(out_dir, "meta_otu_ancombc.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(meta_otu[, c("taxon", "studies", "estimate", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value", "adjusted_p", "tau_squared", "I_squared", "Q_p_value")], row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

pooled <- meta_otu[!is.na(meta_otu$estimate), ]

  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +

  geom_point(shape = 23, size = 4, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = direction_colours, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Pooled effect size per OTU", subtitle = "Random-effects meta-analysis of ANCOM-BC log fold changes; k = number of studies; * adjusted p < 0.05",
       x = "Pooled log fold change, C2 versus C1, with 95% confidence interval", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9))
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "meta_otu_ancombc.png"), meta_plot, width = 10, height = 0.34 * nrow(pooled) + 2.4, dpi = 180)
print(meta_plot)

One cladogram for all included studies, coloured from the ANCOM-BC results

What a cladogram shows. The taxonomy drawn as a tree: the inner ring is the kingdom, each step outwards is a lower rank (phylum, class, order, family, genus), and the outer nodes are the OTUs. Every OTU is labelled with its number and genus, and the phylum (bold) and family are written on the inner nodes.

One tree, all included studies, two conditions. All OTUs that ANCOM-BC analysed are in one tree. Outside the tree there is one ring of tiles per included study (G1 innermost). A tile is salmon when the OTU is higher in C1 in that study and teal when it is higher in C2; it is strongly coloured when the difference is significant and pale when it is not, and it is missing when the study has no usable estimate. The tree nodes show the pooled result of the included studies: salmon or teal when the pooled effect is significant, olive when it is not. A shaded sector marks each significant OTU.

142

Turn the taxonomy of the OTUs into tree coordinates: one row per node with its rank, its position around the circle and its parent.

R code
features <- unique(ancom$feature)
ranks <- cbind(tax_matrix[features, c("Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus"), drop = FALSE], OTU = unname(taxon_label[features]))
ranks <- ranks[do.call(order, as.data.frame(ranks)), , drop = FALSE]
paths <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(ranks)), function(level) apply(ranks[, seq_len(level), drop = FALSE], 1, paste, collapse = ";"))
leaf_position <- seq_len(nrow(ranks))
nodes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(ranks)), function(level) {
  first <- match(unique(paths[, level]), paths[, level])
  data.frame(path = paths[first, level], level = level - 1, name = ranks[first, level],
             position = as.numeric(tapply(leaf_position, factor(paths[, level], levels = unique(paths[, level])), function(p) mean(range(p)))),
             parent = if (level == 1) NA else paths[first, level - 1])
}))
nodes$feature <- ifelse(nodes$level == 6, rownames(ranks)[match(nodes$path, paths[, 7])], NA)
nodes$parent_position <- nodes$position[match(nodes$parent, nodes$path)]
143

Colour the tree nodes from the pooled ANCOM-BC effect sizes. A higher-rank node takes a colour when all the significant OTUs below it point the same way.

R code
nodes$direction <- as.character(meta_otu$direction[match(nodes$feature, meta_otu$feature)])
for (i in which(is.na(nodes$feature))) {
  below <- rownames(ranks)[paths[, nodes$level[i] + 1] == nodes$path[i]]
  hits <- setdiff(unique(as.character(meta_otu$direction[match(below, meta_otu$feature)])), "Not significant")
  nodes$direction[i] <- if (length(hits) == 1) hits else "Not significant"
}
nodes$direction <- factor(nodes$direction, levels = names(direction_colours))
144

Make the ring tiles: one tile per OTU and study, coloured by the condition in which the OTU is higher.

R code
tiles <- ancom[ancom$usable, ]
tiles$position <- match(tiles$feature, rownames(ranks))
tiles$ring <- 8.9 + 0.55 * match(tiles$study, studies)
tiles$higher_in <- ifelse(tiles$lfc_C2_vs_C1 > 0, "C2", "C1")
tiles$significant <- tiles$p_value < significance_level
145

Draw the cladogram and save it.

coord_polar() bends the tree into a circle. Adding 2 to every rank leaves an open ring in the centre, so the inner nodes are not crowded. Tip labels are turned so that they can be read from the outside.

R code
n <- nrow(ranks)
tips <- nodes[!is.na(nodes$feature), ]
angle <- 90 - 360 * (tips$position - 0.5) / n
tips$hjust <- ifelse(angle < -90, 1, 0)
tips$angle <- ifelse(angle < -90, angle + 180, angle)
inner <- nodes[nodes$level %in% c(1, 4), ]
sectors <- tips[tips$direction != "Not significant", ]
branches <- nodes[!is.na(nodes$parent), ]
ring_labels <- data.frame(position = 0, ring = 8.9 + 0.55 * seq_along(studies), label = studies)
cladogram_plot <- ggplot(nodes) +
  geom_rect(data = sectors, aes(xmin = position - 0.5, xmax = position + 0.5, ymin = 2, ymax = 8.4, fill = direction), alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(data = branches, aes(x = position, xend = position, y = level + 1, yend = level + 2), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = branches, aes(x = parent_position, xend = position, y = level + 1, yend = level + 1), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(position, level + 2, fill = direction, size = is.na(feature)), shape = 21, colour = "black", show.legend = c(fill = TRUE, size = FALSE)) +
  geom_tile(data = tiles, aes(position, ring, fill = paste("Higher in", higher_in), alpha = significant), width = 0.9, height = 0.5, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = ring_labels, aes(position, ring, label = label), size = 2.4, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_label(data = inner, aes(position, level + 2, label = name, fontface = ifelse(level == 1, "bold", "plain")), size = 3,
             vjust = -0.6, fill = "white", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0, label.padding = unit(0.08, "lines")) +
  geom_text(data = tips, aes(position, 12.1, label = name, angle = angle, hjust = hjust, fontface = ifelse(direction == "Not significant", "plain", "bold")), size = 3.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = direction_colours, drop = FALSE, name = NULL,
                    labels = c("Higher in C1", "Higher in C2", "Not significant")) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.3)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 3, `FALSE` = 5)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.5, n + 0.5)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 18)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "x", clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Cladogram of all included studies, coloured by condition",
       subtitle = paste0("Tree nodes: pooled ANCOM-BC result. Rings ", paste(studies, collapse = ", "), " (inside to outside): condition in which the OTU is higher in each study (strong colour = p < 0.05)")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 10), legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA), plot.margin = margin(10, 30, 10, 30)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5)))
ggsave(file.path(out_dir, "ancombc_cladogram.png"), cladogram_plot, width = 12, height = 12.5, dpi = 180)
print(cladogram_plot)

Effect size of alpha diversity across the included studies

The idea. The same random-effects model is applied to alpha diversity. For each index and study the effect size is the mean difference, C2 minus C1; its variance comes from the spread within each condition. The quality-control rule here is that a study needs a variance above 0 to be weighted.

Keep in mind. One study group was filtered at 97% identity and the others at 99%. Differences between studies may therefore reflect filtering as well as biology.

146

Calculate the C2-minus-C1 difference and its variance for every index and study.

R code
alpha_effects <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(alpha_metrics), function(metric) do.call(rbind, lapply(studies, function(s) {
  x <- alpha[alpha$study == s, metric]
  data.frame(metric = metric, study = s, effect = mean(x[4:6]) - mean(x[1:3]), variance = var(x[1:3]) / 3 + var(x[4:6]) / 3)
}))))
print(alpha_effects, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

147

Pool the included studies for every index with a random-effects model.

A study in which all six samples have the same value has a variance of 0 and cannot be weighted, so it is left out.

R code
alpha_models <- lapply(setNames(names(alpha_metrics), names(alpha_metrics)), function(metric)
  rma(yi = effect, vi = variance, data = alpha_effects[alpha_effects$metric == metric & alpha_effects$variance > 0, ], method = "REML"))
meta_alpha <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(alpha_models), function(metric) { model <- alpha_models[[metric]]
  data.frame(metric = metric, studies = model$k, estimate = as.numeric(coef(model)), ci_lower = model$ci.lb, ci_upper = model$ci.ub,
             p_value = model$pval, tau_squared = model$tau2, I_squared = model$I2) }))
write.csv(meta_alpha, file.path(out_dir, "meta_alpha.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
print(meta_alpha, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)

148

Draw the forest plots of the four indices and save them.

R code
forest_alpha <- function() {
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.5, 2, 3, 2))
  for (metric in names(alpha_models)) {
    model <- alpha_models[[metric]]
    forest(model, slab = alpha_effects$study[alpha_effects$metric == metric & alpha_effects$variance > 0], header = "Study",
           xlab = "Difference, C2 minus C1", main = alpha_metrics[[metric]], colout = "black",
           col = condition_colours[[ifelse(coef(model) > 0, "C2", "C1")]], border = "black")
  }
  par(old_par)
}
forest_alpha()
png(file.path(out_dir, "meta_alpha_forest.png"), width = 2400, height = 1500, res = 180)
forest_alpha()

Check your understanding

What does a low IQC score tell you about a study?

That its co-abundance structure (which OTUs rise and fall together) differs from that of the other studies more than they differ from each other. Combining such a study with the others mixes different things, which is why MetaQC excluded G4.

Why can no study pass CQC or AQC here, and is that a reason to exclude all of them?

Consistency and accuracy need a clear C1-versus-C2 signal in each study, and three samples per condition cannot give one. It is a limit of the data, not of the studies, so the decision rests on IQC, which does not depend on the condition labels.

Why is ANCOM-BC run separately in each study instead of on one merged table?

Studies differ in sequencing depth, filtering and population. On a merged table those differences can look like differences between conditions. Run per study, each estimate compares C1 and C2 within the same study, and the meta-analysis then combines the estimates.

Why was LEfSe replaced by ANCOM-BC?

With three samples per condition LEfSe’s first test cannot pass after adjustment, so it reports nothing. ANCOM-BC corrects for compositional bias and gives every OTU an effect size with a standard error, which is exactly what a meta-analysis needs.

What is the difference between a fixed-effect and a random-effects model, and what does REML do?

A fixed-effect model assumes every study measures the same true effect. A random-effects model lets the true effect differ between studies and estimates how much (tau²). REML is the method used to estimate tau²; with few studies it is less biased than plain maximum likelihood.

Otu16 is not significant in any single study, but it is in the pooled analysis. How is that possible?

Each study alone is too small to give a precise estimate. All three estimates point the same way, and combining them gives a narrower confidence interval than any single study has.

One study group was filtered at 97% identity. Why does that matter for the pooled results?

A looser threshold keeps different reads, so a difference between G5 and the other studies may come from the filtering and not from biology. In the forest plot of Otu05, G5 is the one study that points the other way, and leaving it out makes the pooled effect significant.

Glossary

16S rRNA gene
A gene found in all bacteria. Parts of it are nearly identical everywhere (good for primers) and parts vary between groups (good for telling bacteria apart).
Read pair
Two sequences read from opposite ends of the same DNA fragment: forward (R1) and reverse (R2).
Contig
One sequence made by joining an overlapping forward and reverse read.
FASTA / FASTQ
Text formats for sequences. FASTQ also stores a quality score for every base.
Count table
mothur file recording how many times each unique sequence occurs in each sample.
Chimera
An artificial sequence made of two different templates during PCR.
OTU
Operational taxonomic unit: a cluster of sequences that are at least 97% similar.
ASV
Amplicon sequence variant: one exact unique sequence treated as a feature.
Phylotype
A group of sequences that share the same taxonomic name.
Shared file
mothur's feature table: one row per sample, one column per OTU, ASV or phylotype.
Relative abundance
A feature's count divided by the sample's total, so samples of different depth can be compared.
Subsampling (rarefying)
Randomly drawing the same number of reads from every sample to equalise depth.
Alpha diversity
Diversity within one sample (observed OTUs, Shannon, inverse Simpson).
Beta diversity
Difference in composition between two samples (for example Bray–Curtis).
PCoA
Principal coordinates analysis: a map of samples in which map distance approximates dissimilarity.
PERMANOVA
A permutation test of whether groups of samples differ in composition, based on a distance matrix.
Chao1
An estimate of the true number of OTUs in a sample, including those that were probably missed, based on the OTUs seen only once or twice.
Bray–Curtis
A distance between two samples based on OTU abundances; dominated by the common OTUs.
Canberra
A distance based on abundances in which every OTU has the same weight, so rare OTUs matter.
Jclass
The Jaccard distance on presence or absence: the share of OTUs that the two samples do not have in common.
ThetaYC
The Yue & Clayton distance, which compares community structure using the proportions of all OTUs.
PERMDISP
A permutation test of whether the samples of one group are more spread out than those of another.
MetaQC
An R package that scores each study of a meta-analysis on six quality measures (IQC, EQC, CQCg, CQCp, AQCg, AQCp) to decide objectively which studies can be combined.
IQC
Internal quality control: whether a study has the same co-abundance structure as the other studies (homogeneity).
CQC
Consistency quality control: whether a study ranks features (CQCg) or groups (CQCp) by their difference between conditions in the same order as the other studies combined.
REML
Restricted maximum likelihood, the method metafor uses by default to estimate the between-study variance tau².
ANCOM-BC
A differential-abundance method that corrects for the bias of compositional data and reports a log fold change with a standard error for each feature.
Effect size
How large a difference is, as opposed to how certain it is. Here: the log fold change of an OTU, or the C2-minus-C1 difference of a diversity index.
Log fold change
The natural logarithm of the ratio between two abundances. 0 means equal; 0.69 means twice as much.
Forest plot
A figure showing the estimate and confidence interval of each study and the pooled estimate underneath.
Cladogram
A tree drawing of the taxonomy, used here to show where the differing OTUs sit.
p-value adjustment (BH)
The Benjamini–Hochberg correction, which limits false discoveries when many tests are run.
Random-effects meta-analysis
Pooling of estimates from several studies while allowing the true effect to vary between them.
Exploratory
Useful for learning and for generating ideas, but not strong enough to support a firm conclusion.

Microbiome hands-on workshop. Side-by-side edition: the mothur steps are unchanged from the original workshop material; the R analysis shows the five studies together, with MetaQC quality control, ANCOM-BC per study in place of LEfSe, and a random-effects meta-analysis (REML). Figure colours follow Marzouk et al., npj Parkinson’s Disease 2025.
